Electrical discharge machining of nickel-based superalloys is sensitive to electrode material because electrode properties affect process efficiency, accuracy, and surface finish. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Studies that compare different graphite grades on Hastelloy C-22 report that finer-grained graphite yields lower surface roughness while coarser grains increase material removal rate but also raise relative tool wear. (Nowicki et al. 2022) A later investigation that repeats this comparison for negative polarity confirms that fine-grained POCO AF-5 (1 µm) improves process efficiency and reduces tool wear relative to coarser POCO EDM-180 (10 µm). (Nowicki et al. 2024)

Experimental work links the dominant EDM parameters to MRR, TWR and Ra: discharge current and pulse duration are repeatedly identified as primary drivers of MRR and Ra, while the off-time (time interval) strongly governs relative electrode wear for graphite electrodes. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024) Taguchi-based factorial analyses in related EDM studies likewise find peak current (amperage) to explain the largest share of variance in MRR and surface roughness in high-performance alloys. (Nas & Kara 2022)(Akıncıoğlu 2022)

The mechanism by which graphite grain size influences performance is attributed to grain detachment affecting discharge stability: detaching grains perturb the spark behavior and thereby modulate removal efficiency and tool consumption. (Nowicki et al. 2024) Surface morphology and electrode end geometry also change under unstable sparking, producing rounded electrode ends from originally sharp square electrodes, which increases wear and dimensional inaccuracy in machined features. (Ramabalan et al. 2024)

Researchers have tested several process modifications to moderate high TWR and low MRR typical of EDM. Approaches include cryogenic treatment of workpiece or electrode, powder-mixed dielectric, ultrasonic assistance, and combinations such as cryogenic cooling with other aids; these hybrid methods target MRR, TWR, surface integrity and recast layer formation. (Shastri et al. 2022) Evidence from nanopowder- and cryogenically treated electrodes shows substantial reductions in electrode wear and overcut in other material systems, indicating that process environment and electrode treatment are potent levers for improving dimensional accuracy. (Sana et al. 2024)

Despite the body of work on graphite and on process aids, comparative data on copper and composite electrodes specific to EDM of Hastelloy are not present in the reviewed sources.

Electrical discharge coating (EDC) literature offers a broader context for modifying surface characteristics via discharge processes, but does not supply direct comparative metrics for conventional versus composite tool electrodes on Hastelloy. (Liew et al. 2020) Overall, the assembled studies converge on peak current and pulse timing as chief determinants of MRR and Ra, and on electrode material microstructure (graphite grain size) and discharge stability as key factors controlling tool wear. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024)
rows.b:
Electrical discharge machining of nickel‑based alloys is sensitive to the electrode material because the electrode’s physical and mechanical properties influence process efficiency, accuracy and the machined surface state; this influence is emphasised in studies on Hastelloy C‑22 that test graphite electrodes of differing grain sizes. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Graphite with coarser grains was found to give higher removal efficiency but also greater relative tool wear, whereas finer‑grained graphite produced lower surface roughness (Ra); empirical models relating machining parameters to MRR, TWR and Ra were derived from these experiments. (Nowicki et al. 2022) A later investigation that introduced fine (1 µm) and coarser (10 µm) POCO graphite grades corroborates that fine‑grained graphite improves machining efficiency and reduces tool wear, and reports that detached graphite grains disrupt discharge stability and hence affect process performance. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

Across the reviewed work, electrical parameters dominate variations in MRR, TWR and surface finish. Peak current (amperage) and pulse duration are repeatedly reported as primary drivers of MRR and Ra, with studies attributing most of the variance in these responses to current in ANOVA results. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Experimental investigations on Hastelloy and other nickel alloys show that pulse duration and current shape both the energy per discharge and the thermal diffusion at the gap, thereby affecting electrode tapering, wear length and edge rounding through unstable sparking and heat diffusion. (Ramabalan et al. 2024) Taguchi and ANOVA analyses in separate EDM studies likewise identify peak current as the single most influential factor on MRR and TWR, often explaining the majority of variation in those outcomes. (Nas & Kara 2022) Similar findings in machining titanium link amperage strongly to MRR and TWR, reinforcing the central role of current in determining process performance. (Akıncıoğlu 2022)

Several approaches have been explored to mitigate the principal EDM drawbacks—high tool wear, low MRR and poor surface integrity. Reviews summarise hybrid strategies such as cryogenic treatment, powder‑mixed dielectrics, ultrasonic assistance and combined process modifications as means to improve MRR, reduce TWR and alter recast formation. (Shastri et al. 2022) Experimental work that mixed nanopowders in the dielectric and applied cryogenic treatment to electrodes reports substantial reductions in electrode wear and overcut for brass electrodes under particular dielectric conditions. (Sana et al. 2024) Separately, electrical discharge coating (EDC) methods extend EDM toward surface modification and coating formation, indicating a broader role for discharge‑based techniques in controlling surface characteristics. (Liew et al. 2020)

Selective laser melting (SLM) produces near-full-density components by layerwise melting and fusion of metal powder using a high power-density laser, and therefore generates characteristic thermal histories that strongly influence the resulting microstructure. (Yap et al. 2015) The rapid cooling intrinsic to SLM gives rise to very fine submicron features: one study reports an average submicron grain size of $0.31\ \mu$m consistent with cooling rates on the order of $10^{7}\ \mathrm{K/s}$ and a martensitic matrix containing dense, needle-shaped nanoprecipitates of Ni$_3$X (X = Ti, Al, Mo). (Tan et al. 2018) Other reviews attribute the distinct hierarchical (sub)grain structure and fine precipitates produced by laser powder bed fusion to the process acting as an intrinsic, in situ heat treatment that both forms and modifies phases during build. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

Heat treatment routes applied after SLM alter precipitate populations, residual stresses and mechanical anisotropy, and thereby change both strength and corrosion-related properties. Systematic characterization of as-fabricated and heat-treated SLM maraging steel shows that post-build aging promotes Ni$_3$X precipitation that accounts for age hardening, while heat treatments relieve residual stress and can reduce layerwise mechanical anisotropy. (Tan et al. 2018) Comparative studies that apply conventional solution treatment and aging before additional surface treatments (for example, nitriding) find that prior heat treatment influences the morphology and integrity of subsequent layers formed by thermochemical processes: nitriding without prior aging produced cracks in the compound layer, whereas nitriding after prior heat treatment improved wear and corrosion resistance relative to untreated SLM material. (Godec et al. 2021)

Reversion of martensite to austenite during intercritical tempering has been investigated as a route to recover ductility and to change corrosion performance. Tempering within the mixed $\alpha'+\gamma$ range produces reversed austenite that precipitates preferentially at martensite lath boundaries, driven by local nickel enrichment originating from dissolution of intermetallics. (Khan et al. 2022) In chloride-containing media, specimens tempered to produce such reversed austenite showed improved pitting behaviour: the intercritically tempered material exhibited a higher pitting potential, reduced corrosion current density and a lower measured corrosion rate in 3.5 wt% NaCl than as-printed, conventionally aged, or homogenized specimens lacking reversed austenite. (Khan et al. 2022)

Surface condition and residual roughness from SLM also modulate corrosion response. SLM-fabricated maraging steel presents a fine martensitic structure in the as-printed state with a relatively high surface roughness (reported Ra ≈ 10 µm), and electropolishing can substantially reduce roughness (by about 65%) while heat treatment and precipitation state are key drivers of both nano-hardness and corrosion potential. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)(Tan et al. 2018) Broad reviews of AM steels note that the unique microstructural evolution during processing can enhance corrosion resistance relative to conventional routes in some cases, but that ductility and fatigue remain challenging and interactions between microstructure, surface condition and corrosion deserve further targeted study. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)(Afkhami et al. 2019)
rows.b:
Selective laser melting (SLM) produces near-full-density maraging steel parts by layerwise melting of powder with a high-power laser, a process that yields very high cooling rates and distinctive microstructures compared with conventional routes. (Yap et al. 2015) Electron microscopy studies of SLM 18Ni-300 (grade 300) report an ultrafine martensitic matrix with submicron grain size (average ~0.31 μm), consistent with cooling rates on the order of $10^{7}\,\mathrm{K/s}$, and a dense distribution of needle-shaped nanoprecipitates (Ni$_3$X, X = Ti, Al, Mo) inside the martensite which contribute to age hardening. (Tan et al. 2018) Scanning electron and EBSD characterization has shown that as-printed SLM maraging steel commonly exhibits a fine martensitic structure with limited texture and similar microstructure across build sections (xy, xz, yz). (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Heat treatments applied to SLM maraging steel modify both precipitate state and residual stress. Systematic characterization indicates that aging produces the massive Ni$_3$X precipitates which strengthen by Orowan looping and coherency strain, while post-build heat treatments relieve residual stresses and can reduce build-orientation mechanical anisotropy. (Tan et al. 2018) Studies comparing as-printed, austenitized-and-quenched, and aged conditions find that precipitation controls both hardness and electrochemical behaviour: aging produces peak nano-hardness and influences corrosion potential. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) Plasma-nitriding experiments performed at temperatures equivalent to aging (520 °C) demonstrate that prior heat treatments affect the morphology and integrity of thermochemical layers: nitriding without prior aging led to cracks in the compound layer, whereas nitriding after suitable prior heat treatment improved wear and corrosion resistance of the AM material relative to untreated AM counterparts. (Godec et al. 2021)

Austenite reversion (reversed austenite) can be induced by intercritical tempering in SLM maraging steels and has a measurable effect on pitting performance in chloride environments. Intercritical tempering near the $\alpha' + \gamma$ range produced reverted austenite that precipitated primarily at martensite lath boundaries, nucleated by local Ni enrichment after dissolution of intermetallics. (Khan et al. 2022) Electrochemical testing in 3.5 wt% NaCl showed that specimens tempered at 720 °C with reverted austenite exhibited a higher pitting potential, lower corrosion current density, and lower corrosion rate than as-printed, aged, or homogenized specimens lacking reverted austenite, indicating an improvement in pitting resistance associated with the reversed austenite state. (Khan et al. 2022)

Reviews of AM steels emphasize that the unique hierarchical (sub)grain structures and fine precipitates formed in AM often enhance strength, wear, and corrosion resistance relative to conventional materials, while challenges remain for ductility and fatigue. (Haghdadi et al. 2020) Surface condition and processing parameters—such as surface roughness and heat-treatment path—also influence corrosion performance, and electropolishing has been shown to reduce SLM maraging steel surface roughness substantially, with implications for corrosion behaviour. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)(Afkhami et al. 2019)

Rooftop solar adoption literature identifies a mix of economic, informational, technical and institutional barriers that interact to slow household uptake. Financial constraints recur across contexts: studies report that upfront cost and the perceived long‑term cost–benefit balance weigh heavily in household decisions, with subsidies and low operating costs acting as the primary financial motivators that mitigate initial investment risk. (Parsad et al. 2020) In low‑income or income‑constrained settings, flexible payment mechanisms and financing options substantially increase uptake by making systems affordable over time. (Aarakit et al. 2021) Evidence from Pakistan and other surveys similarly attributes a negative effect of perceived cost on willingness to adopt, reinforcing the centrality of affordability. (Tanveer et al. 2021) India’s national targets for solar capacity establish a policy backdrop that recognizes rooftop PV as a key component, but achieving such goals requires overcoming these financial barriers. (Goel 2016)

Policy instruments and subsidies therefore play a dual role: they reduce the effective upfront price for households and signal governmental commitment, which in turn shapes investor and consumer confidence. Research using structural models and machine learning ranks policy subsidies among the strongest motivators for household PV investment, alongside environmental and maintenance‑cost considerations. (Parsad et al. 2020) At the same time, country‑level reviews underline that despite ambitious national policies, implementation challenges and broader constraints can limit the translation of targets into household installations. (J & Majid 2020) Case studies of pilot projects show that local rollout encounters practical barriers that policy design alone does not resolve. (Kappagantu et al. 2015)

Awareness, technical knowledge and perceived risks also feature as important non‑financial inhibitors. Survey‑based analyses identify technical barriers and gaps in knowledge as significant predictors of the decision to invest, while perceived risks and doubts about self‑efficacy reduce willingness to adopt. (Parsad et al. 2020)(Tanveer et al. 2021) These informational deficits interact with distributional and equity concerns: qualitative and mixed‑methods work highlights demographic and spatial inequities in who benefits from household solar, suggesting that outreach and inclusive program design are necessary to avoid reinforcing existing disparities. (Sovacool et al. 2022)

Context matters: empirical analyses find heterogeneity across rural versus urban households, grid access, income, housing type and education, with affordability and payment flexibility particularly decisive for rural adoption. (Aarakit et al. 2021) Reviews of national‑level constraints similarly stress that despite abundant solar resource potential, a coherent response must address institutional, technical and market‑level impediments rather than relying on resource endowments alone. (Khare et al. 2013) Taken together, the literature indicates that reducing upfront costs via subsidies or finance, improving awareness and technical support, and tailoring institutional mechanisms to local contexts are complementary priorities for increasing household rooftop solar adoption. (Parsad et al. 2020)
rows.b:
Rooftop photovoltaic (PV) adoption by households in India is constrained by a mix of financial, informational, technical and institutional barriers identified across empirical and review literature. Financially, the high upfront cost and concerns about returns reduce willingness to invest: survey analysis in Kerala finds that government subsidies are the dominant motivator because they reduce the initial investment risk, while low prices and maintenance costs help address concerns about long‑term returns. (Parsad et al. 2020) Evidence from other contexts similarly links upfront cost and perceived financial risk to lower adoption likelihood. (Tanveer et al. 2021)

Affordability interacts with payment design: nationally representative household data from Uganda show that flexible payment mechanisms increase uptake among income‑constrained households and that affordability strongly shapes the type of system adopted, with rural households particularly sensitive to payment terms. (Aarakit et al. 2021) Those findings imply that without financing innovations or staggered payments, many households will defer rooftop PV even where the technology is technically viable. (Aarakit et al. 2021)

Awareness and technical knowledge also operate as inhibitors. The Kerala analyses used structural equation modelling and an artificial neural network to show that technical barriers and low levels of knowledge or awareness significantly predict investment decisions, indicating that non‑financial factors can be as important as subsidies in shaping household choices. (Parsad et al. 2020) Survey work in an Indian pilot smart‑grid site reports user concerns captured through consumer questionnaires about space, consumption patterns and experience with rooftop systems, pointing to gaps in practical information for potential adopters. (Kappagantu et al. 2015)

Institutional and policy barriers appear at multiple scales. National targets for solar capacity set an ambitious policy agenda, but reviews highlight "issues & challenges" in meeting grid‑connected rooftop targets and identify a set of constraints hampering renewables deployment that go beyond resource availability. (Goel 2016)(Khare et al. 2013) Policy reviews note that while governmental programs and liberal investment climates have accelerated renewable markets in India, a range of obstacles affecting deployment remain and merit targeted policy responses. (J & Majid 2020)

Equity and geographic variation further complicate uptake. Comparative work on household solar adoption identifies demographic and spatial inequities that can arise as solar scales, suggesting that distributional impacts, local supply chains and neighbourhood effects influence who adopts and when. (Sovacool et al. 2022) Taken together, the evidence indicates that overcoming delays in rooftop solar adoption requires addressing upfront cost and financing modalities, strengthening information and technical support for households, and resolving policy and institutional frictions that limit effective implementation of national targets. (Parsad et al. 2020)(Aarakit et al. 2021)(Goel 2016)

rows.a:
The evidence for clinical effectiveness of diabetes self-management apps is heterogeneous. A systematic synthesis of app interventions across health behaviors found that most included studies reported statistically significant behavior change, but all carried some risk of bias and the authors called for larger, higher-quality randomized trials to confirm clinical benefits. (Zhao et al. 2016) A pragmatic multicentre randomized trial of the FDA-cleared BlueStar app did not detect a difference in HbA1c between intervention and control arms at three months, although an exploratory analysis found that greater individual app use was associated with small reductions in HbA1c. (Agarwal et al. 2018) A pilot of a gamified app for younger users increased daily glucose monitoring frequency but the authors noted that demonstrating HbA1c improvement would require adequately powered, longer studies. (Cafazzo et al. 2012)

Engagement and retention vary widely across studies and settings. Across the review of app-based interventions, most studies achieved intervention-group retention of 60%–100%, with many above 65%, indicating that reasonably high short-term retention is achievable in trials. (Zhao et al. 2016) However, real-world usage in the BlueStar trial was low overall and differed markedly by clinical site, with median days of use ranging from 9 to 36 over 14 weeks, suggesting that context and implementation strongly influence sustained engagement. (Agarwal et al. 2018)

Multiple design and contextual features are linked to sustained use and to behavior change. The review identified repeatedly that features reducing time burden, intuitive interfaces, real-time feedback, individualization and involvement of health professionals appear to improve effectiveness. (Zhao et al. 2016) User-centred design choices—such as automated transfer of glucometer readings, immediate trend analysis with suggested causes and remedies, social community elements and gamified rewards—were associated with increased monitoring frequency and high user satisfaction in a pilot study. (Cafazzo et al. 2012) Qualitative work with diverse smartphone owners identified nine themes affecting adoption and continued use, including barriers, motivators, credibility, personalization, reminders and sharing, which map onto behaviour-change theories and can guide feature selection. (Peng et al. 2016) App-content reviews also found that many commercial diabetes apps prioritise logging and reminders over personalised education or therapeutic support, indicating design gaps to address for longer-term self-management. (Izahar et al. 2017)

App quality, trust and clinical endorsement shape uptake. Concerns about variable app quality and the need for regulatory or certification mechanisms have been emphasised alongside practical criteria such as content quality, usability, device connectivity and privacy. (Boulos et al. 2014) In interviews with people with type 2 diabetes, recommendation by health professionals and clinician engagement with app data helped adoption, while lack of clinician discussion and limited awareness were common barriers; participants also recommended stronger educational, monitoring and nutritional features. (Jeffrey et al. 2019)
rows.b:
Mobile apps for type 2 diabetes self-management show mixed evidence on clinically measured glycaemic outcomes and more consistent signals relating engagement to any observed benefit. A multicentre pragmatic randomized trial of the BlueStar app did not find a difference in HbA1c between intervention and control arms at three months, though an exploratory analysis reported that each additional day of app use was associated with a small decrease in 3‑month HbA1c ($-0.016$ points per day of use), indicating a dose–response relationship between individual usage and glycaemic change. (Agarwal et al. 2018)

Reports of impact from other diabetes app evaluations emphasise intermediate behaviours rather than direct HbA1c effects. A pilot of a gamified app for adolescents with diabetes increased the frequency of blood glucose monitoring by 50% over 12 weeks, but the authors concluded that demonstrating HbA1c improvement would require larger, longer trials that tie incentives to decision-making as well as monitoring. (Cafazzo et al. 2012) Across broader app interventions targeting health behaviours, a majority of included trials found statistically significant behavioural changes and many interventions achieved retention rates of 60%–100% in intervention groups, suggesting that behaviour change is achievable even when clinical outcomes are not yet consistently shown. (Zhao et al. 2016)

Engagement varies markedly by context and is shaped by both individual and system-level factors. Usage in the BlueStar trial differed by clinical site, with median logins ranging from 9 to 36 days over 14 weeks, demonstrating that setting and implementation influence sustained use. (Agarwal et al. 2018) The larger synthesis of health-app trials likewise notes generally high variability in study quality and retention, and highlights self-monitoring, real-time feedback and individualized content as common ingredients of effective interventions. (Zhao et al. 2016) Qualitative work with adults with diabetes identifies facilitators such as visual trend displays, intuitive navigation and convenience, and barriers including lack of awareness of apps, limited clinician involvement, and practical constraints like connectivity and literacy. (Jeffrey et al. 2019)

Design features associated with adoption and continued use emerge repeatedly in user-centred research and app inventories. Focus-group analysis distilled nine themes important to users, including credibility, personalized information, tracking for awareness, reminders and goal setting. (Peng et al. 2016) An evaluation of commercial diabetes apps found most emphasised reporting and reminders but under‑provided personalised education or therapeutic support, suggesting a mismatch between common app features and user desires for actionable, individualized care tools. (Izahar et al. 2017) Concerns about app quality, data security and the need for regulatory or curated app libraries have been raised in reviews of the app landscape, indicating that perceived credibility and certification may also influence sustained uptake. (Boulos et al. 2014)

Entrepreneurship supported by microfinance is associated with improvements across several empowerment domains, though effects vary by dimension. A mixed-method quasi-experimental study found that women who run enterprises show higher economic, psychological and—less consistently—social and political empowerment than non-entrepreneurs, while qualitative interviews reinforced that entrepreneurship can be an effective route to broader empowerment. (Khan et al. 2022)

Empirical work highlights that empowerment operates at multiple levels and that different interventions influence these levels unevenly. A Three-Dimensional Model distinguishes personal (micro), relational (meso) and societal (macro) empowerment and emphasises that time and cultural context shape when changes appear on each dimension; the model therefore recommends that programs specify which dimension(s) they target and that evaluations separate these outcomes. (Huis et al. 2017)

Household decision-making and the relational aspects of empowerment depend strongly on social networks and local norms. A seven-year quasi-experiment in rural India shows that women's ties to family and community boost ICT use, entrepreneurial entry and profits, whereas ties to men in power can inhibit these outcomes; ICT provision amplified entrepreneurship most for women with strong centrality in local networks. (Venkatesh et al. 2017) Complementary qualitative work finds that socially attuned business processes—those that enable women's economic activity while accommodating local norms—can alter the social order and thereby extend the reach of empowerment beyond individual entrepreneurs. (Haugh & Talwar 2014)

However, credit alone can be insufficient and, in some contexts, harmful. Ethnographic evidence from Bangladeshi villages documents instances where microfinance increased indebtedness and aggravated economic and social vulnerabilities, partly by undermining social capital that supports entrepreneurial capabilities. (Banerjee & Jackson 2016) At the institutional level, the movement toward commercialization raises questions about whom microfinance serves: large comparative analyses indicate that commercially oriented providers may struggle to reach the poorest without subsidised, mission-driven institutions. (Cull et al. 2009) A broad literature review further shows that microfinance research spans many topics—sustainability, products, targeting and impact assessment—highlighting persistent gaps in linking financial provision to consistent enterprise growth and sustained household empowerment. (Brau & Woller 2004)

Together, these findings suggest that while microfinance-facilitated entrepreneurship can foster business growth and multiple forms of empowerment, outcomes depend on the design of interventions, social network position, local norms, and institutional incentives; standalone credit provision therefore often falls short of producing uniform gains in household decision-making and societal-level empowerment. (Khan et al. 2022)(Huis et al. 2017)
rows.b:
Microfinance-supported entrepreneurship yields mixed but instructive evidence on business growth and women's empowerment. A quasi-experimental mixed-methods study comparing women entrepreneurs and non-entrepreneurs in a limited geographic area reports that entrepreneurs exhibit stronger economic, psychological and overall empowerment indicators than non-entrepreneurs, while gains in political and social domains are smaller. (Khan et al. 2022) Haugh and Talwar document that entrepreneurial innovations which align with local social norms can enable women's economic participation and, in some cases, contribute to shifts in the social order that expand women's agency. (Haugh & Talwar 2014) Together these findings indicate that business activity often increases personal and economic capacities but that social and political dimensions of empowerment may lag. (Khan et al. 2022)(Haugh & Talwar 2014)

The evidence also highlights how non-financial factors condition entrepreneurial success. A seven-year quasi-experiment in rural India shows that women's social ties and access to ICT interact with each other and with time to shape both the initiation of enterprises and profit outcomes, with family and community ties amplifying the positive effects of ICT on entrepreneurial activity and profit trajectories. (Venkatesh et al. 2017) Haugh and Talwar's qualitative work similarly emphasizes that entrepreneurship which respects local cultural constraints can nonetheless reconfigure social relations in ways that enable women's participation. (Haugh & Talwar 2014) These studies imply that credit alone does not determine enterprise outcomes; social networks, information access, and culturally sensitive business models matter. (Venkatesh et al. 2017)(Haugh & Talwar 2014)

Reviews and critiques further qualify expectations about microfinance as a route to sustainable empowerment. A systematic review of the microfinance literature notes a broad research base on MFI sustainability, products and impact assessment but signals that microfinance has not been fully integrated into mainstream entrepreneurial finance scholarship. (Brau & Woller 2004) A critical ethnography of Bangladeshi villages finds that market-based microfinance can increase indebtedness and exacerbate vulnerabilities, thereby undermining the social capital that might otherwise support entrepreneurship. (Banerjee & Jackson 2016) These perspectives caution that scaling credit without attention to institutional missions, subsidies, or client targeting can limit benefits for the poorest women. (Brau & Woller 2004)(Banerjee & Jackson 2016)

Conceptual work recommends parsing empowerment to interpret heterogeneous results and to guide program design. A Three-Dimensional Model distinguishes personal (micro), relational (meso) and societal (macro) empowerment and stresses that time and culture influence when and how each dimension emerges following an intervention. (Huis et al. 2017) Empirical findings above align with this model: micro-level gains in beliefs and actions often precede relational and societal changes, and interventions combining finance with information, network support, or socially attuned business practices yield stronger enterprise and empowerment outcomes. (Khan et al. 2022)(Venkatesh et al. 2017)(Haugh & Talwar 2014)

Market and institutional economics also matter for policy choices: analyses of the global microfinance industry show that commercialization can expand outreach but that institutions with explicit social missions—often subsidized—are better positioned to serve the poorest clients. (Cull et al. 2009)

rows.a:
Household-level studies converge on four recurring frictions that interrupt the pathway from awareness to rooftop installation: information deficits, procedural complexity, structural constraints, and financial risk perceptions. In Karnataka, qualitative interviews and questionnaires with 70 households identify space and roof-ownership limits as the most frequently cited obstacle among non-adopters, with information gaps and upfront cost following behind. (Bagla 2026) The same study documents a large divergence between anticipated and experienced procedural difficulty: prospective adopters expected complexity at a mean of $5.1$ out of $10$ but reported actual complexity of $2.2$ after installation, indicating that perceived process difficulty is often greater than the lived experience. (Bagla 2026) Bagla also reports that some households describe a "subsidy paradox" in which vendor restrictions, empanelment rules and paperwork reduce the effective value of capital subsidies. (Bagla 2026) A summary statement in that study situates these four frictions as constraining adoption despite Karnataka’s comparatively progressive policy framework. (Bagla 2026)

Studies from other contexts reiterate and nuance these themes. A purposive-sample case study of three villages finds that rural households often view solar PV as low-cost and environmentally friendly but simultaneously doubt its reliability, fear theft, and regard the upfront investment as prohibitively large; the authors recommend targeted awareness campaigns and financing designs that accommodate low-income rural families. (Chidembo et al. 2022) Survey work in Patna identifies resident-reported barriers that align with the Karnataka findings and argues that coordinated action across government, energy providers and the public is necessary to raise uptake. (Kumar 2025) Similarly, a large cross-India survey using diffusion-of-innovation constructs reports that perceived complexity, relative advantage, compatibility and observability are significant predictors of household purchase intention for rooftop systems. (Kumar & Kaushik 2022)

Perceptions of subsidies and incentives interact with these frictions. In North Kerala, awareness of government subsidy programs correlates positively with attitudes toward rooftop installation and with intention, alongside environmental concern and cost–benefit perceptions, though the authors note that these variables explain only part of the variance in intention. (N.M & A.H 2026) Empirical work from Karnataka complicates this picture by showing that almost half of adopters (45.8%) would have installed even without the subsidy, while others feel procedural restrictions and vendor rules dilute subsidy value. (Bagla 2026) Local studies of consumer perceptions likewise spotlight trust and technological reliability as determinants of adoption, suggesting that policy measures must address both concrete constraints (roof space, paperwork) and subjective barriers (trust, perceived energy quality). (Panwar & Yadav 2026)

Across these studies, evidence is consistent that informational and procedural perceptions frequently overstate actual installation difficulty, but structural limits and upfront finance remain binding for many households; targeted outreach, simplified processes and finance options are recurrently proposed remedies. (Bagla 2026)(Kumar & Kaushik 2022)(Chidembo et al. 2022)
rows.b:
Household-level evidence from Karnataka highlights four interlocking frictions between awareness and installation: information gaps, procedural complexity, structural limits on roofs, and perceived financial risk. Bagla reports that even in a progressive policy environment with capital subsidies under PMSGY, adoption remains low; the study used semi‑structured interviews and questionnaires with 70 households in Karnataka (24 adopters, 46 non-adopters) to probe these barriers. (Bagla 2026) Bagla summarises the barriers as informational, procedural, structural and perception-related, noting that anticipated complexity among potential adopters substantially exceeded the complexity actually experienced after installation. (Bagla 2026)

Procedural complexity appears salient in households’ narratives but is experienced differently by adopters and non‑adopters: before installation adopters expected complexity at a mean of $5.1$ out of $10$, while after installation they reported actual complexity of $2.2$, a $57$ per cent reduction. (Bagla 2026) At the same time, some adopters described a "subsidy paradox" in which limitations on eligible panels, vendor empanelment rules and paperwork reduced the practical value of subsidies for many households. (Bagla 2026)

Structural constraints—roof space and roof‑ownership—rank highest among non‑adopters in the Karnataka sample, ahead of information and upfront cost. (Bagla 2026) Complementary evidence from rural contexts shows that households may view PV as attractive on environmental and cost grounds yet worry about reliability, theft and high initial capital outlay, concerns that can deter adoption unless programmes explicitly address them. (Chidembo et al. 2022) Surveyed households in Meerut similarly emphasise cost, trust and technological reliability as determinants of adoption decisions. (Panwar & Yadav 2026)

Perceptions and social‑psychological factors also shape uptake. A TPB‑based study in North Kerala found that environmental concern, awareness of government subsidies and cost–benefit perceptions positively affect attitudes toward rooftop systems, and that attitude, subjective norms and perceived behavioural control significantly predict installation intention, with attitude the strongest predictor. (N.M & A.H 2026) At a broader level, diffusion‑of‑innovation analysis across India finds that perceived relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, observability and other innovation dimensions are associated with households’ purchase intentions, though "trialability" did not predict intent in that sample. (Kumar & Kaushik 2022)

City‑level and rural studies converge on the need for coordinated action: research in Patna argues that overcoming barriers requires collaboration among government, utilities and consumers to build trust and create supportive systems for adoption. (Kumar 2025) Taken together, the literature portrays rooftop uptake as limited less by single factors than by overlapping informational, procedural, structural and perceptual frictions that interact with programme design and local contexts. (Bagla 2026)(Chidembo et al. 2022)
